newsitem.title: USA: Digital sees gross margin unaffected by price cuts.
newsitem.headline: Digital sees gross margin unaffected by price cuts.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp expects no erosion of its gross margins after moving to slash prices on its line of servers and workstations powered by its 64-bit Alpha microprocessors, a senior vice president said on Thursday.
"Top-line, we don't expect this to have any impact on our gross margins," Harry Copperman, vice president of Digital's systems business unit told Reuters.

Copperman said decreases of about 40 percent a year in memory chip prices have allowed Digital to pass on its savings to customers, while manufacturing efficiencies and expected volume increases should also help offset the impact of the price cuts on margins, he said.

Digital specifically mentioned rivals Sun Microsystems Inc and Compaq Computer Corp in announcing the price cuts of up to 40 percent or more. Copperman said Digital is looking to take market share away from its competitors.
"Our expectation is this will allow us to increase share," he said. "This price announcement clearly ups the ante for our competitors."
Digital has long boasted a technological edge over its competitors with its fast 64-bit Alpha microprocessor, but has had difficulty converting that leaderership into sales.

According to Andrew Allison, publisher of the newsletter Inside the New Computer Industry, revenue from Digital's Alpha systems running on the Unix operating system grew by about 50 percent in 1996. But Digital still only accounted for 8.9 percent of the RISC/Unix market last year.

Competition is growing even more intense as many of Digital's established competitors in the RISC/Unix landscape, including Sun, IBM Corp and Hewlett-Packard Co, have introduced or are about to ship their own 64-bit microprocessors.
In addition to Compaq, systems based on Microsoft Corp's Windows NT operating system and Intel Corp's chips, together known as "Wintel," are making headway in the market, analysts said.
"You've seen us for the last two years assert our leadership in terms of performance," Copperman said. "Now you're seeing the company become very aggressive in terms of price leadership."
Even though its competitors are coming with their own 64-bit chips, Copperman said Digital was the only company ready to offer a complete 64-bit package including the necessary application software.
Cooperman said he expected the price cuts to motivate many of Digital's customers to buy more memory and move up to higher-end products.
